clue.text: Crack jokes finally with character in Wonderland

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word jokes

parts.note: the Hatter (the Mad Hatter) is a character in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland

explanation.surface: Someone finally cracks a few jokes while playing a part in Wonderland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' looks like the verb for telling jokes, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To shatter something is to break it into pieces, a stronger synonym of crack as a verb.

clue.text: Second best riot

parts.note: the cream is the best part, as in the cream of the crop

explanation.surface: A second outbreak of disorder is the worst yet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'riot' is the informal sense: someone very funny.
explanation.definitionFit: A riot and a scream are both informal words for a hilariously funny person or thing.

clue.text: Has it cut me after removing tops? Sharp!

indicators.note: tops are the first letters, which in a down clue sit at the top of each word

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a knife has cut them: that was sharp!
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the first letter of each word leaves AS, T, UT, E.
explanation.definitionFit: Astute means shrewd and quick-witted, the mental sense of sharp.

clue.text: Intimidated teen nastily in series of internet messages

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters within the run of messages

parts.note: a thread is a chain of posts on a forum or social media

indicators.note: nastily suggests the letters of teen are handled roughly and mixed up

explanation.surface: A teenager is bullied online in a chain of nasty messages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nastily' gives TENE, an anagram of 'teen'; a thread is a chain of replies on a forum.
explanation.definitionFit: To threaten is to menace someone, so threatened is a synonym of intimidated.

clue.text: Seed around small bird's shelter

indicators.note: around has the source word wrapped about the abbreviation

parts.note: a seed and a root are both the source or origin of something
S is the abbreviation for small, as in clothing sizes

explanation.surface: Seeds scattered round a small bird's shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seed' and 'root' share the sense of an origin.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is a perch or place where birds settle to sleep.

clue.text: Loads get moved inside these pubs without argument

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the pubs wrap around the argument

parts.note: a bar is a pub or drinking place
a row is a quarrel or argument

explanation.surface: Drinks are carted from pub to pub without anyone falling out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here is the old sense of outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrow is a small cart that carries loads, so heavy items are moved about inside one.

clue.text: Bravo — I have changed our way of acting

parts.note: Bravo is the NATO alphabet word for B

indicators.note: changed means altered, so the letters of I have are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone cheers that they have reformed their conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'changed our way of acting', but only I HAVE is rearranged, into EHAVI; 'our' is kept as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Behaviour is the way a person conducts themselves, literally their way of acting.

clue.text: Unusual stuffing for a recipe

indicators.note: stuffing is what fills the middle, so the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: An odd stuffing called for in a recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stuffing' looks like a cooking noun; it signals letters inside 'for a recipe'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare means seldom found or occurring, a direct synonym of unusual.

clue.text: Heads embracing sanctimonious views

indicators.note: embracing means holding within arms, so the outer word wraps around the other

parts.note: onion is old slang for head, as in off one's onion
pi is short for pious, meaning sanctimonious

explanation.surface: Leaders who hold self-righteous opinions.
explanation.walkthrough: ONION for head is British slang, as in 'off your onion', meaning mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Opinions are personal views or beliefs, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Most sugary dessert is French

parts.note: sweet is the British word for a dessert or pudding
est is French for is

explanation.surface: A French dessert is declared the sweetest of all.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a 'sweet' is the pudding course.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweetest is the superlative of sweet, meaning containing the most sugar.

clue.text: Something on an aircraft maybe that spins both ways

indicators.note: both ways says the word spells the same whichever end you start from

parts.note: a part that spins round an axis is a rotating part, the role this word names

explanation.surface: A description of a spinning aircraft part that turns in both directions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spins both ways' has a second reading: the word reads the same forwards and backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A helicopter's rotor is the spinning blade assembly that lifts it, so it is an aircraft part, the 'maybe' marking one example.

clue.text: Apart from that parent, Mike's left with Ernie?

indicators.note: Mike's left reads as Mike has gone away, so that letter departs from the parent

parts.note: a mother is a parent
Mike is the NATO alphabet word for M
Ernie Wise was the straight man of the British comedy double act Morecambe and Wise

explanation.surface: A parent called Mike has left the family and moved in with someone named Ernie.
explanation.walkthrough: Ernie Wise was half of Morecambe and Wise, a much-loved British comedy duo.
explanation.definitionFit: Otherwise is an adverb meaning in other respects, which is what apart from that expresses.

clue.text: Tasty, fatty tart regularly full of beans

indicators.note: regularly asks for every other letter of the words fatty tart

parts.note: someone full of beans is lively and active

explanation.surface: A rich tart, full of beans, sounds like a tempting dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of 'fatty tart': A, T, T, R.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasty is informal for good-looking, so it is a synonym of attractive.

clue.text: Garment some flipping Scot likes

indicators.note: flipping says the hidden letters are read backwards
some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A Scotsman approves of a garment, with 'flipping' as a mild expletive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like a mild swear word but tells you to read the hidden letters right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilt is a knee-length pleated tartan skirt, the traditional Highland garment.

clue.text: Mean child who's naughty and overaggressive? Not half!

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous, naughty child

indicators.note: not half says only half the word is wanted, here its back half

explanation.surface: A spiteful child who is naughty and too aggressive, with 'Not half!' as emphatic agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', but here drops OVERAGG, half of the fourteen letters. 'Mean' is slang for excellent, as in a mean cook.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal use mean signals skill, as in plays a mean guitar, so it means impressive.

clue.text: Devon temples demolished for housing estates?

indicators.note: demolished buildings are knocked down and rebuilt, so the letters get a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Old West Country places of worship are knocked down to make way for new housing estates.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a housing estate as one example of a development.
explanation.definitionFit: A development is a group of new buildings on one site, and housing estates are an example.

clue.text: Urged to go after former lover spoke

indicators.note: to go after places the urging word behind the former partner

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
pressed means urged or insisted

explanation.surface: Someone was encouraged to chase an old flame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoke' is the past of speak, matching 'expressed', voiced in words.
explanation.definitionFit: To express a thought is to put it into words, so expressed is a synonym of spoke.

clue.text: After school, avoid going over timetable

indicators.note: after puts the reversed word behind the school abbreviation
going over in a down clue reads as turning upside down, so the word is reversed

parts.note: to elude is to avoid or escape

explanation.surface: A pupil dodges going over the timetable after school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going over' reverses ELUDE to EDULE.
explanation.definitionFit: A schedule is a timetable listing when things happen.

clue.text: Fire is in Greene novel

indicators.note: in places the small word within the rearranged name
novel means new, so the letters of Greene are made into something fresh

explanation.surface: A fire breaks out in a Graham Greene novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like the noun for Graham Greene's book, but is the anagram signal, making ENERGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To fire someone up is to energise them, so fire as a verb is a synonym.

clue.text: Modern company with new caretaker?

parts.note: a caretaker government or manager is a temporary one, holding office until a permanent one arrives

explanation.surface: A modern firm takes on a new caretaker for its building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caretaker' is the adjective (a caretaker manager), meaning temporary, not the janitor the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Contemporary means belonging to the present day, a close synonym of modern.

clue.text: Unemployed group of students after university education

indicators.note: after places the student group behind the university letter

parts.note: the NUS is the National Union of Students, the British student body

explanation.surface: Students graduate from university only to find themselves out of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unemployed' is not jobless here but not put to use.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unused has not been employed in the sense of used, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Article to post assuming costs primarily go up

parts.note: A is the indefinite article

indicators.note: assuming means taking on, so the posting word takes the letter into itself

parts.note: to post a letter is to send it

indicators.note: primarily picks the first letter of costs

explanation.surface: Posting an article, assuming the costs will mostly rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'assuming' means taking on, so SEND holds C.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascend is to climb or rise, a formal synonym of go up.

clue.text: Take home large vase, we're told

indicators.note: we're told says the word is heard spoken rather than written

parts.note: an urn is a large vase

explanation.surface: Someone carries a large vase home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take home' sounds like carrying something, but it is pay: take-home earnings.
explanation.definitionFit: To take home a sum is to earn it as net pay, so the phrase is a synonym.

clue.text: Shows sign of uncertainty around gifts

indicators.note: around signals turning the hesitation word round to face the other way

parts.note: er is the sound of someone hesitating, unsure
presents are gifts

explanation.surface: Someone hesitates over a pile of gifts, unsure what they are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Er' is the sound of hesitation; 'around' turns it the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: To represent something is to depict or show it, so represents is a synonym of shows.

clue.text: Meeting, in truth, not exciting at first

indicators.note: not means without, so the letter is taken away from the word

parts.note: really means in truth or truly

indicators.note: at first picks out the opening letter of exciting

explanation.surface: A dull meeting, honestly not exciting at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes E from REALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: A rally is a mass meeting held to support a cause.

clue.text: Cheese could make female fed up

indicators.note: up in a down clue reads the word from bottom to top

parts.note: fed and ate are both past tenses of eating

explanation.surface: Cheese would make a woman sick of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fed up' looks like bored, but 'up' turns ATE into ETA.
explanation.definitionFit: Feta is a crumbly white Greek cheese made from sheep's or goat's milk.

clue.text: Blanket unravels badly, one's admitted

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so the numeral goes inside the jumbled letters
something done badly is messed up, so the letters of unravels are jumbled

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone confesses their knitted blanket is coming apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unravels badly' is the anagram: UNRAVELS rearranged gives UNVERSAL, which takes in I. 'Blanket' is an adjective here, as in blanket ban.
explanation.definitionFit: A blanket rule applies to everything, so it is universal in scope.

clue.text: Send out children

definitions.meaning: to send it out or distribute it
a legal and formal word for a person's offspring

explanation.surface: An instruction to send the children outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue means to distribute officially, and also means descendants, as in died without issue.

clue.text: Leader's shot carrying Muirfield's first green

indicators.note: carrying means holding, so the reshuffled letters hold another inside
shot means wrecked or ruined, so the letters of leader are thrown out of order
first picks out the opening letter of Muirfield

explanation.surface: A golf leader's shot at Muirfield lands on the green.
explanation.walkthrough: Muirfield is a Scottish championship golf course. 'Leader's' is 'Leader is', with 'shot' scrambling LEADER into EERALD, which holds M.
explanation.definitionFit: Emerald is a vivid bright green, the colour of the gemstone.

clue.text: Conceded defeat — what cricketer perhaps did with change in opener

indicators.note: change in opener says the first letter is swapped for a different one

parts.note: a cricketer, perhaps, fielded: caught or stopped the ball

explanation.surface: A cricket team gives up, and an opening batsman is changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opener' sounds like the opening batsman, but means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to give way or surrender, so yielded matches conceded defeat.
